findings.title: change_password no longer follows the session-rotation pattern that reset_confirm_post copies

intent_doc_match.quote: **Fix:** `change_password` now rotates `session_secret`, invalidating all other sessions on password change while re-issuing the acting user's cookie (CWE-613). Supersedes v2.6 threat decision T-58-07/AR-58-02 (was *accept*, now *mitigate*). ... **Note:** Track A's reset-confirm session rotation deliberately mirrors this `change_password` pattern.
intent_doc_match.assessment: The intent doc does not allow this change. It records the rotation as a deliberate security fix and calls it the reference pattern for reset-confirm. The diff reverses that decision and no new decision record replaces it.

findings.problem: The codebase has an established way to change credentials: rotate session_secret with generate_session_secret(), persist it together with the new hash, then re-sign the acting user's cookie with sign_session plus COOKIE_MAX_AGE and is_secure_request. setup_post (routes.py ~1294-1341) and reset_confirm_post (routes.py ~1941-2009) both do this, and STATE.md names change_password as the source of the pattern. This diff removes all of it from change_password only. Credential changes now behave inconsistently: a password reset logs out other devices, but a normal password change does not.
findings.fix_hint: Restore the generate_session_secret() rotation and the cookie re-issue under the new secret, matching reset_confirm_post. If dropping it is intended, record a new threat decision that supersedes the v2.8.1 mitigation and update the reset-confirm note.
findings.why_it_matters: After this change, a session cookie that may be compromised stays valid after the owner changes their password. That reverses a shipped CWE-613 fix and splits two flows that are documented to behave the same way.

members.title: Stolen session cookies retain access after password changes
members.problem: Changing only password_hash preserves the signing secret, so an attacker holding a pre-change triggarr_session cookie can still access protected routes after the owner changes their password. AuthMiddleware accepts that cookie at triggarr/web/middleware.py:145-148 without checking the password hash; validate_session in triggarr/auth.py checks only its signature and 30-day expiry. The removed rotation previously revoked these cookies immediately, and no replacement revocation check protects this path.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},
members.why_it_matters: Changing only password_hash preserves the signing secret, so an attacker holding a pre-change triggarr_session cookie can still access protected routes after the owner changes their password.
members.fix_hint: Restore atomic session-secret rotation with the password update and reissue the acting user's cookie under the new secret. Verify that another device's pre-change cookie is rejected.

members.title: Password change no longer rotates session_secret, so a hijacked session cookie stays valid after the password is changed
members.problem: The diff removes a security control. change_password used to call generate_session_secret() and save the new secret together with the new hash. Now it updates only password_hash. Sessions are checked with validate_session(cookie, auth.session_secret) at routes.py:1357, so every cookie signed before the change still passes after it. Someone holding a stolen cookie keeps access, which defeats the usual reason for changing a password. I found no other code that does this job for the password-change path: the only other rotation is in the reset flow (routes.py:1941-2009), which this endpoint does not reach. Existing tests check for the removed behavior and will now fail: tests/test_auth_routes.py:604 (test_change_password_rotates_session_secret_and_persists) and tests/test_auth_integration.py:183 (pre-change cookie must be evicted).
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},
members.why_it_matters: If a session was compromised, changing the password no longer locks the attacker out. The two existing tests that check this will also fail.
members.fix_hint: restore session_secret rotation in the model_copy update and re-issue the acting user's cookie signed with the new secret (as the reset flow does at routes.py:1941-2009)

members.title: Changing the password no longer logs out other sessions: a stolen session cookie stays valid for up to 30 days
members.problem: The diff removes the session-secret rotation from POST /settings/password. The new code copies only password_hash and keeps the existing session_secret. Session cookies are signed over the username and session_secret only (auth.py:79), checked in middleware.py:146 with validate_session, and the 30-day COOKIE_MAX_AGE comes from auth.py:10. Nothing binds a cookie to the password hash. So after this diff, any triggarr_session cookie issued before the password change keeps authenticating every route until it expires. session_secret is rotated only in initial setup (routes.py:1294) and in the reset flow (routes.py:1941). The diff adds no other session-invalidation mechanism.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},
members.why_it_matters: An attacker holding a stolen cookie keeps full access to the Radarr/Sonarr control UI and settings (including API keys) for up to 30 days after the owner changes the password to lock them out.
members.fix_hint: Restore the generate_session_secret() rotation in change_password and re-issue the acting user's cookie, mirroring reset_password at routes.py:1941-2009.

members.title: Password-change endpoint no longer rotates session_secret, so stolen/compromised sessions survive a password change
members.problem: The diff deletes the session_secret rotation (and the matching re-issued cookie for the acting user) from change_password, leaving only the password_hash update. Session cookies are HMAC-signed via sign_session/validate_session (triggarr/auth.py:79-115) using only session_secret and username -- they carry no reference to password_hash. Since session_secret is left unchanged, every cookie signed before the password change continues to validate after it, including one held by an attacker who prompted the password change in the first place.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},
members.why_it_matters: This is a reversion: commit 0866332 added exactly the code this diff removes, closing a documented finding (reports/security-2026-04-15.md, SHIELD-008, CWE-613). The regression test tests/test_auth_integration.py::test_password_change_invalidates_old_sessions will now fail. The sibling /reset/confirm endpoint still rotates session_secret, so /settings/password is now the inconsistent, vulnerable one.
members.fix_hint: restore session_secret rotation (generate_session_secret(), fold into new_auth's model_copy update) and re-issue the acting user's cookie signed with the new secret, mirroring the still-intact /reset/confirm flow at triggarr/web/routes.py:1937-1967

The diff changes only routes.py, so these tests are expected to fail.
